name: dict
why: The RFC 2229 dictionary protocol is an old, forgotten network protocol, and the client is a fair door into it.

brief.what_it_is: The dict package is a client for the DICT Dictionary Server Protocol, defined in RFC 2229, according to the Homebrew description. The homepage at dict.org/bin/Dict is not documentation for this client. It is the public web search form for the DICT server, offering search types such as exact headword, prefix, substring, suffix, regular expression, SOUNDEX, and Levenshtein distance one. You enter a term and pick a database, and get back definitions. The Homebrew executable list also includes dictd, dictfmt, dictunformat, dictzip and related tools, so the package is broader than a bare client.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no framing for this client. The only stated purpose is the Homebrew description: a client for the RFC 2229 dictionary protocol. The scout note calls the protocol an old, forgotten network protocol and the client a fair door into it, but that is the scout's wording, not the project's.
brief.install_notes: Nothing was seen beyond the Homebrew formula metadata. No install steps, configuration, or first-run instructions were on the pages I read. The executable list suggests the formula also installs the dictd server and dictfmt dictionary-building tools.
brief.standout: The protocol is old and niche, and the package bundles a client with server and dictionary-compiling tools. The public dict.org server is still live and serves many dictionaries, including WordNet, the Jargon File, the Free On-line Dictionary of Computing, and CC-CEDICT, so the client can be tried against a real server.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows database versions dated into 2026 (CC-CEDICT 20260906, an English-German devel release dated 2026-01-09), which suggests the public server is actively maintained. I found no release date, last commit, or maintenance note for the dict client package itself.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a web search form, not a project README, so I could not confirm how the client is used, what platforms it supports, or its licence. I did not see a README or docs for the client. The scout's claims about the protocol are unverified by the pages I read. The package also includes server components (dictd), which goes beyond the client the description names.

entry.title: dict
entry.tldr: A command-line client for RFC 2229, the old dictionary protocol, with a live public server and tools to host or build your own dictionaries.
entry.deeper_look:
dict speaks the DICT protocol, defined in RFC 2229. You ask a server for a word, name a database, and get definitions back as plain text over a network connection. The Homebrew description calls it a client for exactly that.

The public server behind dict.org is still live. Its web form, which is the project's homepage, offers search strategies such as exact headword, prefix, substring, suffix, regular expression, SOUNDEX, and Levenshtein distance one. The brief says it serves many dictionaries, including WordNet, the Jargon File, the Free On-line Dictionary of Computing, and CC-CEDICT. Version dates on that page run into 2026, so the server looks maintained.

The formula installs more than a client. The executable list includes dictd (a server), dictfmt and dictunformat (for building and converting dictionary data), and dictzip (a compression tool). That makes it a small door into the whole idea: a lookup service with its own wire protocol, dictionary file format, and server, all from an era when each such service got its own protocol.

The brief found no README or docs for the client itself, so the details of usage are left to the tool's own help output.
entry.install:
brew install dict
# also installs the dictd server and dictfmt tools; the client needs network access to a DICT server
